playbooks.title: Build your first useful agent
playbooks.goal: Turn one narrow task into a versioned prompt agent, then inspect its behavior in the live lab before adding tools or orchestration.

steps.title: Choose the smallest useful task
steps.description: Define the user, expected output, what the agent must not do, and whether a managed prompt loop is enough.

steps.title: Choose the correct SDK and endpoint
steps.description: Identify project management, model inference, and agent invocation boundaries. Match the example to the current service and package version.

steps.title: Bind an existing model and explicit identity
steps.description: Use a model deployment you actually have, confirm project RBAC, and keep tokens and keys out of code and browser storage.

steps.title: Create a version and run a bounded smoke
steps.description: Use a small non-sensitive prompt. Record the selected agent version, completion state, and token usage; preserve the previous version.

steps.title: Create quality evidence before expanding scope
steps.description: Define representative cases and a rubric. A successful response proves connectivity, not accuracy or production readiness.

pitfalls: Do not assume a demo agent can browse or inspect your subscription without explicit tools.
Add each tool only with a documented permission and approval boundary.
The live lab is a user-triggered, billable demo, not an anonymous public API.

playbooks.title: Deploy a hosted agent
playbooks.goal: Use a supported direct-code or container deployment path, bind the intended Foundry project, and make deployment reproducible.

steps.title: Identify the current hosting contract
steps.description: Start with the current quickstart and supported runtime/protocol. If lifting an old preview app, read the migration guide first.

steps.title: Prefer direct code when it fits
steps.description: Use codeConfiguration for supported source deployment. Choose a Dockerfile or prebuilt image only for actual container-specific requirements.

steps.title: Resolve identity, project, and network dependencies
steps.description: Bind the existing project and model. Decide public versus private access explicitly, including DNS, tool access, and where the deployment runner executes.

steps.title: Deploy a version through OIDC
steps.description: Use the documented azd workflow and a repository/environment-scoped federated identity. Keep project IDs as configuration, never bake bearer tokens into the app.

steps.title: Invoke, evaluate, and retain rollback
steps.description: Invoke the actual deployed protocol endpoint, inspect traces, and compare a versioned evaluation dataset before promotion.

pitfalls: Old agent.yaml and old hosted endpoint examples may no longer match the current service.
Creating an agent does not automatically configure private networking or tool permissions.
Code deployment and container deployment have different dependencies and costs; do not provision ACR unnecessarily.

playbooks.title: Build an Agent Framework workflow
playbooks.goal: Build a small, explicit orchestration with measurable tool and handoff behavior instead of starting with an uncontrolled agent swarm.

steps.title: Pin the right language and channel
steps.description: Read the separate Python or .NET release notes and current migration guidance. Optional integrations may remain prerelease even when the core is stable.

steps.title: Run the smallest language-specific sample
steps.description: Start with a supported provider client and one tool. Resolve identity and async/runtime setup before layering on workflow logic.

steps.title: Choose deterministic versus agentic routing
steps.description: Use explicit workflow edges when the business process is known. Use a model-driven handoff only when the task needs that flexibility.

steps.title: Add tool boundaries and human approval
steps.description: Choose MCP for tools and A2A for agent delegation. Design timeout, cancellation, identity, and approval behavior at each boundary.

steps.title: Observe and prove the workflow
steps.description: Trace tool selection and handoffs, test failures and cancellation, then measure task success on held-out scenarios before hosting it.

pitfalls: Agent Framework is not the hosted runtime; the deployment contract is a separate choice.
Do not assume the Python and .NET APIs or release tags move in lockstep.
More agents introduce more failure, latency, state, and cost boundaries.

playbooks.title: Put an AI gateway in front
playbooks.goal: Choose the right API Management offering and put documented identity, policy, routing, and observability around AI traffic.

steps.title: Select a tier and supported protocol
steps.description: Compare existing APIM AI capabilities with the dedicated AI gateway tier. Check preview restrictions, regions, and the backend protocol you actually use.

steps.title: Authenticate both sides
steps.description: Design caller-to-gateway validation and gateway-to-Foundry authentication separately. Confirm issuer, audience, allowed callers, and backend RBAC.

steps.title: Apply explicit usage budgets
steps.description: Choose supported token and rate policies per consumer. Decide how to handle quota errors and avoid unbounded retries or duplicated stateful agent work.

steps.title: Govern tools and failure paths
steps.description: If MCP is involved, validate its supported authentication and publishing path. Test streaming, backend pool behavior, failover, and rejection cases in a lab.

steps.title: Observe without leaking prompts
steps.description: Correlate gateway and agent requests, inspect latency and usage, and deliberately configure content logging, sampling, retention, and alerts.

pitfalls: CORS controls browser access, not authorization.
AI gateway tier preview status is not the status of every APIM AI feature.
The live lab currently calls Foundry directly; this runbook does not mean APIM has been provisioned.

playbooks.title: Evaluate, trace, and improve
playbooks.goal: Turn a demo that responds into an application whose quality, safety, and regressions can be measured.

steps.title: Define the dataset and acceptance criteria
steps.description: Collect representative success, edge, refusal, and failure cases. Separate development and holdout sets, and preserve dataset versions.

steps.title: Choose evaluators that fit the evidence
steps.description: Match groundedness, tool accuracy, task adherence, safety, and custom rubrics to available inputs. Record evaluator and judge-model versions.

steps.title: Establish a baseline and a release gate
steps.description: Compare the candidate to a known-good agent/model/prompt version. Set workload-specific thresholds; do not substitute a nonempty smoke response for quality.

steps.title: Instrument and sample production behavior
steps.description: Configure tracing and continuous evaluation with an explicit privacy and cost policy. Investigate failures, latency, and expensive tool loops.

steps.title: Feed failures back into the next candidate
steps.description: Curate traces into regression cases, run scoped safety scans, and keep the holdout set separate before promoting an improvement.

pitfalls: An evaluator score is meaningful only with its rubric, inputs, version, and dataset.
Evaluation and tracing can add cost and expose sensitive data if configured carelessly.
Keep functional smoke checks, offline quality gates, and continuous evaluation clearly separate.

playbooks.title: Ground answers with Foundry IQ
playbooks.goal: Connect a supported knowledge source, preserve access boundaries, and evaluate whether the agent retrieves and cites the right evidence.

steps.title: Map the source and access model
steps.description: Identify data owners, supported connectors, freshness requirements, and how the user's permissions reach retrieval.

steps.title: Connect the knowledge base
steps.description: Follow the current connection contract and inspect indexing, grounding, and tool authentication instead of assuming the agent can reach every source.

steps.title: Validate the network boundary
steps.description: For a private deployment, verify DNS, private endpoints, tool connectivity, and where ingestion and evaluation execute.

steps.title: Measure retrieval and answer quality
steps.description: Test citations, groundedness, relevance, missing evidence, and permission-sensitive questions against a representative dataset.

steps.title: Operate the knowledge lifecycle
steps.description: Track source changes and stale documents, inspect traces, and turn real retrieval failures into updated regression cases.

pitfalls: A valid citation does not by itself prove that the answer is supported.
Do not assume all connectors implement identical permission trimming or freshness.
Treat source text as untrusted reference material, not instructions to the agent.

scenarios.title: Choose: prompt agent or hosted agent?
scenarios.prompt: I want a small Foundry assistant that answers from approved reference material. Compare a managed prompt agent with a hosted Agent Framework application. Recommend the smallest sensible starting point, list prerequisites, and cite the supplied official sources. Do not claim you inspected my Azure project.
scenarios.expected: A clear agent-type decision, explicit assumptions, official references, and no invented deployment or availability claims.

scenarios.title: Plan a hosted-agent deployment
scenarios.prompt: Plan a hosted-agent deployment for a standard Python Agent Framework app into an existing Foundry project. Compare direct code with container deployment, describe the current configuration and identity/network decisions, then propose OIDC CI/CD, a smoke check, an evaluation gate, and rollback. Cite supplied sources; verify missing runtime or region details rather than inventing them.
scenarios.expected: A code-first deployment plan that distinguishes application packaging, infrastructure, identity, invocation, and quality evidence.

scenarios.title: Design an Agent Framework workflow
scenarios.prompt: Design a small Microsoft Agent Framework workflow that triages a request, retrieves approved knowledge, and asks a human before taking an external action. Explain explicit routing versus model-driven handoffs, state, cancellation, tool permissions, and how to test the workflow. Do not invent current class names or package versions; point to the supplied language-specific samples.
scenarios.expected: A bounded workflow with an approval boundary and testable failure behavior, not an uncontrolled agent swarm.

scenarios.title: Design an APIM AI gateway
scenarios.prompt: Design an API Management AI gateway for a Foundry demo that will later serve multiple authorized teams. Separate caller and backend authentication, token/rate budgets, Responses and streaming compatibility, MCP governance, and telemetry. Distinguish existing APIM AI capabilities from the dedicated AI gateway tier. Cite supplied sources and flag region or preview constraints that need checking.
scenarios.expected: Two explicit trust boundaries, protocol-aware policies, bounded retries, and no assumption that CORS is authentication.

scenarios.title: Build a quality and observability plan
scenarios.prompt: Propose an evaluation and observability plan for this source-grounded Foundry guide assistant. Give representative dataset categories, useful evaluators, example workload-specific acceptance criteria, a holdout strategy, and a trace-to-regression loop. Distinguish functional smoke, offline evaluation, and continuous evaluation. Do not claim an evaluation was run.
scenarios.expected: A versioned, privacy-aware evaluation plan that treats a successful API response as connectivity evidence only.

scenarios.title: Plan a grounded Foundry IQ assistant
scenarios.prompt: Plan a Foundry IQ assistant grounded in approved enterprise documents. Explain supported-source selection, freshness, caller permissions, private tool connectivity, citations, and retrieval evaluation. Treat source text as untrusted data and say which connector-specific details must be verified in current documentation.
scenarios.expected: A retrieval design with explicit freshness and access boundaries, plus a measurable grounding rubric.
